summary: RADIUS has traditionally run over UDP. This experimental RFC defines how to carry it over TCP, to deal with handling problems seen with RADIUS over TLS. TCP is allowed only when a layer such as TLS or IPsec provides confidentiality and security.

plainLanguage.summary: This memo defines how to send unchanged RADIUS packets over TCP. TCP can provide reliable transport, but it does not provide confidentiality, so RADIUS/TCP requires TLS, IPsec, or another secure layer.

subtitle: An experimental way to carry RADIUS over TCP, with TLS or another security layer required.

tldr.problem: RADIUS over UDP can lose packets, require application retransmissions, fragment large packets, and provide no transport-level congestion control or connection status.
tldr.mechanism: The memo carries the unchanged RADIUS packet format over TCP and defines connection monitoring, retransmission, error handling, and port-use rules.
tldr.outcome: The RFC is Experimental. Bare TCP MUST NOT be used without TLS, IPsec, or another secure upper layer; the memo recommends retaining UDP for many NAS-to-server exchanges.

today: RFC 6613 is an Experimental RFC published in May 2012 and was updated by RFC 7930 and RFC 9765. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes it.

sections.title: Why Carry RADIUS over TCP
sections.content:
RADIUS was defined to use UDP. The memo identifies several limitations: UDP is unreliable, so RADIUS implementations use application-level timers and retransmissions; large RADIUS packets can fragment; UDP does not tell the client when a connection is down; and UDP provides no congestion control.

The main motivation for TCP is to address transport issues in inter-server RADIUS/TLS communication. The memo notes that TCP can handle large payloads and provide reliable delivery, which can help multi-round-trip EAP authentication exchanges. TCP is specified separately from TLS so transport and security remain distinct.
sections.plainLanguage: UDP does not confirm delivery or signal that a connection has failed. TCP can provide reliable delivery, which may help RADIUS exchanges between servers.

sections.title: Where TCP Is and Is Not Recommended
sections.content:
RADIUS/TCP is aimed at inter-server communication, such as proxy-to-proxy traffic, where there may be enough traffic in both directions to use the TCP connection effectively. For a Network Access Server (NAS) communicating with a RADIUS server, the memo says TCP is usually a poor fit: requests may be too sparse, causing extra acknowledgement and watchdog traffic without corresponding benefits.

For NAS-to-server communication, UDP SHOULD continue to be used. Implementations of RADIUS Dynamic Authorization SHOULD also continue to use UDP because that traffic is usually small. The memo repeatedly states that bare TCP MUST NOT be used without TLS, IPsec, or another secure upper layer.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo mainly targets busy links between RADIUS servers. It recommends UDP for many NAS-to-server exchanges, and requires a separate security layer whenever TCP is used.

sections.title: Packet Format, Ports, and Server Liveness
sections.content:
RADIUS packet format, codes, authenticators, packet lengths, attributes, and related calculations remain unchanged over TCP. The default ports are 1812/tcp for radius, 1813/tcp for radius-acct, and 3799/tcp for radius-dynauth. Ports 1645 and 1646 MUST NOT be used as defaults. For RADIUS/TLS, 2083/tcp (radsec) SHOULD be the default; port 1812 SHOULD NOT be used for RADIUS/TLS.

For liveness, a client MUST mark a connection down when the network stack reports it inactive. If the stack reports it active, the client waits for the application-layer watchdog before deciding it is down. The Status-Server packet is the required watchdog message. A client MUST NOT declare the RADIUS server unresponsive until all TCP connections to it are marked down.
sections.plainLanguage: The RADIUS message itself stays the same, but TCP has assigned default ports. Clients also use a watchdog message to decide whether an active connection is still responsive.

sections.title: Retransmission, Ordering, and Invalid Packets
sections.content:
Because TCP provides reliable transport, implementations MUST NOT retransmit a RADIUS request over the same TCP connection. They also MUST NOT resend it over another connection to the same address and port while the first connection is still considered available. If a connection closes, an unanswered request MAY be sent over a new connection; if its ID changes, security attributes must be recalculated.

TCP can cause head-of-line blocking: loss of one TCP segment delays later segments, even if later RADIUS packets could otherwise be processed. RADIUS's one-octet ID permits at most 256 in-flight packets on a connection. The memo recommends reserving ID zero for Status-Server.

When malformed packets are silently discarded under the RADIUS rules, implementations SHOULD close the TCP connection because decoding later packets depends on correct framing. The memo lists invalid lengths, malformed attributes, and failed authenticator checks among conditions requiring closure.
sections.plainLanguage: TCP already retransmits lost transport data, so the RADIUS application must not retransmit requests on a healthy connection. A malformed packet can make the rest of the stream unsafe to parse, so the connection is closed.

sections.title: Security and Connection Limits
sections.content:
RADIUS packet formats, signing, and client verification do not change, so prior RADIUS security issues remain. Bare TCP does not provide confidentiality or negotiate credible cipher suites; it MUST NOT be used without TLS, IPsec, or another secure upper layer.

Unlimited TCP connections can exhaust system resources. Clients and servers SHOULD support configurable limits on connection counts, connection lifetimes, idle times, and rates of new connections. The memo says it introduces no other known security issues for RADIUS-over-TCP transport at the time of publication.
sections.plainLanguage: TCP does not encrypt RADIUS traffic. A separate security layer is mandatory, and implementations should limit connections to avoid resource exhaustion.
